246.title: Katha Upanishad (one week): Nachiketa and Death (1 of 7)
246.hook: a boy watches his father give away worn-out cows, and asks one question too many
246.carry: choose the good over the pleasant
246.tomorrow: Katha Upanishad (one week): Nachiketa and Death (2 of 7)
246.howItsDone: Hindus tell the Katha's story of Nachiketa to children and also study it closely; Vedanta teachers, Shankara among them, wrote commentaries on it.

segments.voice: Last week, tadvana, the dear one: the victory was never theirs, it was Brahman's. Your line was the one behind the ear. Did you thank someone whose help you didn't see? Day two hundred forty-six.

A charity drive at a big house. The owner is making a show of generosity, and his servants lead the gifts out one by one. But the kid in the doorway notices something. The gifts are the old stuff. Cows that have drunk their last water, eaten their last grass, given their last milk. Cows that will never calf again. Everyone else nods politely. The boy can't. This is how the Katha Upanishad begins: a boy named Nachiketa, a father's careless gift, and, before long, Death.
screen: `A SHOW OF GENEROSITY.` → `THE OLD COWS.` → `THE BOY IN THE DOORWAY.`

segments.voice: The father is called Vajashravasa, and he's performing a sacrifice where you're meant to give away everything you own. But the cows he gives are worn out. The text says it bluntly: they've drunk their water, eaten their grass, been milked dry, and will bear no more. Joyless worlds, it says, await the one who gives gifts like these. Then: shraddha entered the boy. Shraddha is faith, trust, a kind of deep seriousness. You met it in the Gita. It enters Nachiketa, still a child, and he goes to his father. Father, to whom will you give me? Because if the sacrifice means giving everything, then the son belongs on the list. It's a real question and a sharp one. The father doesn't answer. Nachiketa asks a second time. Then a third. And the father, angry, the way a parent can when a child sees through them in front of others, snaps: I give you to Death. To Yama. Stop there. It's an ancient story, and it's also a very modern one. A parent says something in anger they can't take back. A child takes them at their word. Nachiketa doesn't run and hide. He thinks it through: I go first among many, in the middle of many. What will Yama do with me? He sees that all people ripen and fall like grain, and rise again like grain. And he goes. This week is the Katha, and its word is the two paths. We'll reach them on day nine. It starts with a boy who couldn't pretend old cows were a gift.
screen: `THE WORN-OUT COWS.` · `SHRADDHA ENTERED THE BOY.` · `TO WHOM WILL YOU GIVE ME?` · `I GIVE YOU TO DEATH.` · then, large: `NACHIKETA AND DEATH.`

segments.voice: Two minutes. Think of something you've given lately: time, money, attention, help. Be honest, gently. Was it a real gift, or a worn-out one: the leftover hour, the distracted ear, the thing you didn't want anyway? No blame. Just notice. Then think of one real thing you could give this week, something that would cost you a little. Hold it. Breathe with it. The bell holds the time.
Nachiketa. A boy whose father, angry, said: I give you to Death. Shraddha, faith, had entered him, and he went to Yama's house without fear.
Your line: choose the good over the pleasant. Today, when you give something, give the real thing, not the leftover. Day two hundred forty-six.

247.title: Katha Upanishad (one week): Nachiketa and Death (2 of 7)
247.hook: three nights waiting at Death's door, and three wishes
247.carry: choose the good over the pleasant
247.tomorrow: Katha Upanishad (one week): Nachiketa and Death (3 of 7)
247.howItsDone: Hindu tradition treats the honoring of guests as sacred (atithi devo bhava, 'the guest is as God'); the Katha's opening is often told to show even Death keeping that duty.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nachiketa began with old cows and a boy's question: to whom will you give me? To Death. Did you give something real, not the leftover? Day two hundred forty-seven.

A guest arrives, and nobody's home. He waits on the step. One night. Two. Three. Nobody brings him so much as a glass of water. The Katha takes that seriously: in a house where a brahmin guest waits without food, it says, the household's hopes, its good deeds, its children and its cattle are all put at risk. And this house belongs to Death. That's where Nachiketa is sitting, three nights in, still hungry.
screen: `WAITING ON THE STEP.` → `THREE NIGHTS.` → `THE HOUSE OF DEATH.`

segments.voice: Nachiketa reaches Yama's house, and Yama is away. The boy waits three nights without food. When Yama returns, his household tells him: a guest has been waiting, a young brahmin, like fire entering a house. Make him welcome. Yama is appalled. He bows to the boy and says: you stayed three nights in my house without eating. For each night, choose a boon, a wish. Three wishes. It sounds like a fairy tale, and in a way it is, but watch what Nachiketa asks for. The first wish: let my father be calm again, no longer angry with me, and let him know me and welcome me when I'm sent back. That's it. Of all the things to ask of Death, he asks first that the relationship with his father be healed. Yama grants it: your father will sleep peacefully and his anger will be gone. The second wish: teach me the fire ritual that leads to heaven, where there's no fear, no hunger, no old age. Yama teaches it, and is so pleased with how quickly the boy learns that he names the fire after him: the Nachiketa fire. He even gives him an extra gift, a chain or garland. Two wishes down. Each one reasonable, generous, the kind of thing a good son and a serious student would ask. And then the third wish. That's tomorrow. But notice who Nachiketa is so far: a boy who waits, who forgives first, who learns fast. The two paths are about to open in front of him.
screen: `THREE NIGHTS WITHOUT FOOD.` · `A BOON FOR EACH NIGHT.` · `FIRST: LET MY FATHER BE AT PEACE.` · `SECOND: THE FIRE THAT LEADS TO HEAVEN.` · then, large: `AND THE THIRD?`

segments.voice: Two minutes. Nachiketa's first wish wasn't for himself; it was for peace with the person who'd hurt him. Bring to mind someone you're a little estranged from. Not the hardest person; someone where things are just stuck. Imagine them calm, sleeping peacefully, their anger gone. You don't have to do anything about it today. Just let yourself wish them peace, the way the boy did. If it's too hard, choose someone easier. The bell holds the time.
Vara, a boon, a chosen gift. Three nights at Death's door, then two boons: peace with his father, and the fire ritual that leads to heaven.
Your line: choose the good over the pleasant. Today, if you had one wish for someone who's hurt you, make it peace. Day two hundred forty-seven.

248.title: Katha Upanishad (one week): Nachiketa and Death (3 of 7)
248.hook: the third wish, the best bribe ever offered, and a boy who turns it down
248.carry: choose the good over the pleasant
248.tomorrow: Katha Upanishad (one week): Nachiketa and Death (4 of 7)
248.howItsDone: Some Hindu teachers use the Katha's shreyas and preyas, the good and the pleasant, as everyday language for moral choices; the passage opens the second section of the Katha.

segments.voice: Yesterday, vara, a boon for each: three nights at Death's door. Peace with his father, and the fire that leads to heaven. Now the third. Day two hundred forty-eight.

There's a question people rarely say out loud. It comes at funerals, or at three in the morning, or in the hospital parking lot. When someone dies, what happens? Are they still, somewhere? Nachiketa is sitting across from the one being who would actually know. He has one wish left. And he asks it. What happens next turns on a choice that shows up in small ways all day long: the good, or the pleasant.
screen: `THE THREE A.M. QUESTION.` → `ONE WISH LEFT.` → `HE ASKS IT.`

segments.voice: The third wish: when a person dies, there's this doubt. Some say they still are; some say they are not. Teach me this. Yama flinches. Even the gods doubted about this, he says. It's subtle, not easy to know. Choose another wish. Don't press me. Nachiketa doesn't budge: if even the gods doubted, and you say it's hard to know, then there's no teacher like you and no wish like this one. So Death tries a bribe. Sons and grandsons who'll live a hundred years. Herds of cattle, elephants, gold, horses. Land as wide as you like, and as many years as you want. Beautiful companions with chariots and music, rare among mortals. Enjoy them all. Just don't ask me about death. And the boy says: these last only till tomorrow, Death. They wear out the sharpness of the senses. Even a whole life is short. Keep your horses, keep your songs and dances. No one is made content by wealth. Now Yama's tone changes. Many pleasures, he says, did not tempt you. And he teaches the two paths. One is shreyas, the good. The other is preyas, the pleasant. Both come to a person, and both bind. The wise one looks them over, tells them apart, and chooses the good over the pleasant. The foolish one chooses the pleasant, for the sake of getting and keeping. The pleasant isn't evil; it's what feels nice now. The good is what's actually good for you, and it often doesn't feel like much at first. That's our word, and our line. Nachiketa just chose it in front of Death.
screen: `WHEN SOMEONE DIES, WHAT THEN?` · `CHOOSE ANOTHER WISH.` · `KEEP YOUR HORSES AND SONGS.` · `THE GOOD, AND THE PLEASANT.` · then, large: `THE TWO PATHS.`

segments.voice: Two minutes. Think of one choice waiting for you today: the phone or the walk, the extra drink or the early night, the easy reply or the honest one. Picture both paths. The pleasant: feel how it pulls. The good: feel how quiet it is. You don't have to decide now. Just see them clearly, side by side, the way the wise one in the Katha looks them over. Breathe, and let the difference be plain. The bell holds the time.
Shreyas, the good, the better. Paired with preyas, the pleasant: both come to a person, and both bind. The wise look them over and choose the good; Nachiketa turned down the world for his question.
Your line: choose the good over the pleasant. Today, catch one small fork in the road, and take the quieter path once. Day two hundred forty-eight.

249.title: Katha Upanishad (one week): Nachiketa and Death (4 of 7)
249.hook: Death's answer: the self is not born and does not die
249.carry: choose the good over the pleasant
249.tomorrow: Katha Upanishad (one week): Nachiketa and Death (5 of 7)
249.howItsDone: Katha 1.2.18–19, echoed in Bhagavad Gita 2.19–20, is among the verses most often recited at Hindu funerals and memorials as the teaching that the self is not born and does not die.

segments.voice: Yesterday, shreyas, the good, and the pleasant. Your line, choose the good over the pleasant. Did you take the quieter path once? Day two hundred forty-nine.

If you read the Gita with us, today may give you a jolt of recognition. There's a verse you've heard before, in chapter two, when Krishna first tells Arjuna that the self can't be killed. Here it is again, almost word for word. Except now it's not Krishna speaking on a battlefield. It's Death, speaking to a child. The Gita, it turns out, was borrowing from the Katha. Today Yama finally answers the question.
screen: `A VERSE YOU'VE HEARD BEFORE.` → `NOT KRISHNA. DEATH.` → `THE ANSWER.`

segments.voice: Yama says: the knowing self is not born, and does not die. It didn't come from anywhere, and it didn't become anyone. Unborn, eternal, everlasting, ancient: it is not killed when the body is killed. Then: if the killer thinks he kills, and the killed thinks he's killed, neither of them understands. This one does not kill, and is not killed. Those two verses reappear in the Gita, two nineteen and two twenty, with small changes. So Death's answer to what happens when we die is: the self you really are was never born, so it can't die. The body ends. The self doesn't. Then Yama adds something surprising about how this is known. The self is smaller than the small and greater than the great, hidden in the heart of every creature. And it can't be gotten by lectures, or by brains, or by much learning. It's gained by the one it chooses; to that one it reveals its own nature. Commentators read that line in different ways. Shankara hears the seeker choosing the self alone. Theistic teachers like Ramanuja hear grace: the Lord chooses whom to reveal himself to. Both schools agree on the next line: not the one who hasn't turned from wrong, not the restless, not the scattered, can reach it by cleverness. This is why the two paths matter. Choosing the good over the pleasant isn't a rule for its own sake. It's what makes the mind quiet enough to notice what was never born.
screen: `NOT BORN, AND DOES NOT DIE.` · `IT DOES NOT KILL; IT IS NOT KILLED.` · `NOT GAINED BY LEARNING.` · `THE ONE IT CHOOSES.` · then, large: `SMALLER THAN SMALL, GREATER THAN GREAT.`

segments.voice: Two minutes. Sit, and notice what in you has changed over the years. Your body. Your opinions. Your face in photos. Then notice what hasn't: the plain sense of being here, aware. It was here at seven, it's here now. Rest in that for a few breaths. You don't have to decide what it is. Just notice it's the one thing in the room that didn't age. The bell holds the time.
Aja, unborn. The knowing self is not born, and does not die; it is not killed when the body is killed, unborn, eternal, everlasting, ancient.
Your line: choose the good over the pleasant. Today, when you catch yourself restless or scattered, choose one small quiet thing instead. Day two hundred forty-nine.

250.title: Katha Upanishad (one week): Nachiketa and Death (5 of 7)
250.carry: choose the good over the pleasant
250.tomorrow: Katha Upanishad (one week): Nachiketa and Death (6 of 7)
250.howItsDone: Hindu teachers of the Upanishads use the Katha's chariot to explain self, mind and senses, and some pair it with the Gita's picture of Krishna driving Arjuna's chariot.

segments.voice: Yesterday: aja; the self is not born and does not die, and it isn't gained by cleverness. Your line, choose the good over the pleasant. Day two hundred fifty.

Driving home, and arriving with no memory of the drive. Something got the car there, but who, exactly? Or the opposite: the plan was to go straight home, and somehow the car is in the drive-through line. Who was steering? Yama knows the two paths are easy to name and hard to walk. So he gives Nachiketa a picture to carry, with a place in it for every part of a person: the body, the mind, the senses, and someone riding along. A chariot.
screen: `HOME, WITH NO MEMORY OF THE DRIVE.` → `WHO WAS STEERING?` → `A CHARIOT.`

segments.voice: Know the self as the rider in the chariot, Yama says, and the body as the chariot. Know the buddhi, the intellect, the part of you that discerns and decides, as the charioteer. The manas, the everyday mind, is the reins. The senses are the horses, and the things they chase are the roads. Picture the senses as horses: sight, hearing, smell, taste, touch. Each one strong, each one pulling toward whatever it wants. The reins connect them to the charioteer. And the rider, the one the whole trip is for. Then Yama says what happens when it goes wrong. If the charioteer has no understanding, and the reins are always slack, the senses run wild like bad horses. That's the drive-through line. If the charioteer understands and holds the reins steady, the senses are like good horses: all their strength, going where they should. Notice he doesn't say kill the horses. Horses are the power. You need them. The point is who holds the reins. And where does the road go? The one whose charioteer is wise, whose reins are steady, reaches the end of the road, which the text calls the highest place of Vishnu, the all-pervading. That's the two paths in one picture. The pleasant path is letting the horses choose the road. The good path is the charioteer choosing it, and the horses running there gladly. Some readers hear an echo of it in the Gita, where Krishna is Arjuna's actual charioteer.
screen: `THE RIDER, AND THE CHARIOT.` · `CHARIOTEER, REINS, HORSES.` · `WILD HORSES, OR GOOD HORSES.` · `THE END OF THE ROAD.` · then, large: `THE CHARIOT OF THE SELF.`

segments.voice: Two minutes. Sit, and feel your senses as horses. Notice which one is pulling hardest right now: a sound, an itch, hunger, the phone. Don't fight it. Just feel the reins in your hands. Breathe, and imagine gently drawing them in, not yanking, just steadying. Let each horse settle. Then sit as the charioteer, reins held lightly, horses calm, the rider behind you, at rest. The bell holds the time.
Ratha, chariot. Know the self as the rider, the body as the chariot, the intellect as the charioteer, the mind as the reins, and the senses as the horses.
Your line: choose the good over the pleasant. Today, when one sense yanks you toward something, feel for the reins before you follow. Day two hundred fifty.

251.title: Katha Upanishad (one week): Nachiketa and Death (6 of 7)
251.hook: arise, awake; the path is sharp as a razor's edge
251.carry: choose the good over the pleasant
251.tomorrow: Katha Upanishad (one week): Nachiketa and Death (7 of 7)
251.howItsDone: Katha 1.3.14, 'uttishthata jagrata', was taken up by Swami Vivekananda as a call to awaken, and Hindu teachers quote it as a call to wake up to the self.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ratha, the chariot of the self, in one picture. Rider, charioteer, reins and horses. Did you feel for the reins once? Day two hundred fifty-one.

Have you ever been woken by someone who really needed you up? Not a gentle alarm. A hand on the shoulder, a voice: get up, now. There's one verse in the Katha that sounds exactly like that: short, urgent, impossible to sleep through. Swami Vivekananda took it up as a rallying cry for his listeners. It's possible to know the line well without knowing it came from the house of Death.
screen: `A HAND ON THE SHOULDER.` → `GET UP, NOW.` → `FROM THE HOUSE OF DEATH.`

segments.voice: Right after the chariot, Yama says: uttishthata, jagrata. Arise! Awake! Having reached the great teachers, learn. And then a warning: the path is sharp as the edge of a razor, hard to cross, hard to walk, say the wise. A razor's edge: step carelessly and you're cut. That doesn't mean it's cruel. It means it's narrow. Choosing the good over the pleasant isn't done once; it's done step by step, with attention. A few verses later, Yama explains why the path is hard. The self-existent one, he says, pierced the openings of the senses outward. So we look outward, not at the self within. Our eyes, ears and attention point away from ourselves, by design. But some wise person, wishing for the deathless, turned their eyes inward and saw the self. The phrase is often translated as turning the gaze around. And he gives a picture of what's seen: a person the size of a thumb, dwelling in the middle of the body, like a flame without smoke. Lord of past and future. The same today and tomorrow. So here are three ways the Katha says the same thing. Arise, awake: the sleeper drifts toward the pleasant. The razor's edge: the good path is narrow and needs care. The inward gaze: the senses face out, and the good path turns them back. None of it is gloomy. A flame without smoke is a warm picture. It's what's waiting when you stop looking only outward.
screen: `ARISE! AWAKE!` · `SHARP AS A RAZOR'S EDGE.` · `THE SENSES FACE OUTWARD.` · `A FLAME WITHOUT SMOKE.` · then, large: `TURN THE GAZE AROUND.`

segments.voice: Two minutes. Open your eyes and notice how naturally they go outward, to the room, the light, whatever moves. Now close them, and, just for a moment, turn the gaze around. Not looking at anything. Feeling the place you look from. Some people find it helps to picture a small, steady flame in the center of the chest, smokeless and warm. If that picture helps, rest with it. If not, just rest behind your closed eyes. The bell holds the time.
Uttishthata, arise. The good path is sharp as a razor's edge, and it turns the gaze inward. Awake, and learn.
Your line: choose the good over the pleasant. Today, once, when you reach for something outside yourself to feel better, turn inward for one breath first. Day two hundred fifty-one.

252.title: Katha Upanishad (one week): Nachiketa and Death (7 of 7)
252.hook: a tree with its roots in the sky, the knots of the heart, and a boy set free from death
252.carry: choose the good over the pleasant
252.tomorrow: Mandukya Upanishad (12 verses, one week): the four states; om, letter by letter (1 of 7)
252.howItsDone: Students of Vedanta read the Katha with commentaries such as Shankara's; its closing chapter defines yoga as the steady holding of the senses.

segments.voice: Yesterday, uttishthata grew sharp as a razor's edge: arise, awake, turn the gaze around, and find a flame without smoke. Today the Katha ends. Day two hundred fifty-two.

A boy was given to Death by an angry father. He waited three nights hungry at Death's door, turned down every pleasure in the world, and asked the question Death itself didn't want to answer. A story like that could end with a bargain lost, or a little time won before Death comes back. Not this one. Today, the last pages of the Katha. Death finishes teaching. And the boy walks out of Death's house free.
screen: `A BOY AT DEATH'S DOOR.` → `NOT A BARGAIN LOST.` → `THE BOY WALKS OUT FREE.`

segments.voice: Near the end, Yama gives three last pictures. First, a tree: the eternal ashvattha, a sacred fig, with its roots above and its branches below. The world hangs down from what's above it, like a tree upside down. It may sound familiar; the Gita opens chapter fifteen with the same tree. Second, yoga. When the five senses are still, with the mind, and the intellect doesn't stir, that's called the highest state. And Yama defines yoga as that firm holding of the senses. Not a pose. A steadiness. The reins, from the chariot, held firm. Third, the heart. When all the desires that dwell in the heart are let go, the mortal becomes immortal, and reaches Brahman here. When all the knots of the heart are cut, even in this life, then the mortal becomes immortal. That's the whole teaching. Not escape from the world; a heart with its knots untied. And then the last verse. Nachiketa, having received this knowledge from Death, and the whole method of yoga, reached Brahman, free of stain and free of death. And so will anyone, the text says, who knows the self this way. So here's the week. Old cows and a boy's question. Three nights at Death's door. Peace with his father, the fire, and the third wish. The two paths, the good and the pleasant. The self not born, not dying. The chariot. Arise, awake. And the knots of the heart, cut. Choose the good over the pleasant.
screen: `THE TREE WITH ROOTS ABOVE.` · `YOGA: THE SENSES HELD STILL.` · `THE KNOTS OF THE HEART, CUT.` · `NACHIKETA, FREE OF DEATH.` · then, large: `THE TWO PATHS.`

segments.voice: Two minutes. Bring your attention to the center of your chest. Notice if there's a knot there right now: a worry, a want, a grudge. Don't try to cut it. Just breathe toward it, the way you'd breathe on cold hands. Let the senses go still, one at a time: eyes resting, ears resting, the body quiet. That steadiness, the Katha says, is yoga. If the knot loosens even a little, notice that. The bell holds the time.
Ashvattha, the sacred fig with roots above and branches below. Nachiketa chose the good, learned from Death, and walked out free. That's the Katha.
Your line: choose the good over the pleasant. That's the week. Tomorrow, twelve verses and one syllable: om. Today, find one knot in your heart and loosen it a little. Day two hundred fifty-two.
